::: {.lead}
A mining game stores its level as a table: in each tile, the number of gems.
An RPG stores its enemies as a table: one row for each enemy, one column for
each stat. A game engine stores, for every object, a table of 16 numbers
that says where the object is, how it is turned and how big it is. All
these tables are **matrices**. In lectures 2 to 8 you worked with vectors and
angles. In this lesson you meet matrices: how to name their parts, how to add
them and how to multiply them by a number. In lecture 10 you multiply
matrices, and from lecture 11 on they move, turn and scale game objects.
Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary matrix matrix-row matrix-column matrix-size matrix-entry row-vector column-vector transpose square-matrix main-diagonal matrix-addition transformation-matrix >}}

## 9.1 The mine map: what a matrix is

The level designer of *Gem Grid* draws a mine of 3 rows of 4 tiles. Each tile
holds some gems. The programmer needs one name for the whole map, and a clear
way to say "the tile in row 2, column 3". A matrix gives both (@fig-map).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 9.1 — Matrix, size and entry"}
A **matrix** is a rectangular table of numbers in **rows** (across) and
**columns** (down). Its **size** is "rows × columns": a matrix with 3 rows and
4 columns is a 3 × 4 matrix. The number in row *i* and column *j* is the
**entry** $a_{ij}$. The row number always comes first.
:::

![The gem map of *Gem Grid* as a 3 × 4 matrix M. The entry $m_{23}$ (row 2, column 3) is 0.](images/matrix-map.png){#fig-map width=96%}

$$M = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 0 & 6 \\ 1 & 7 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

Matrices are written with a capital letter (M, A, B), and their entries with
the small letter and two numbers: $m_{23}$ is "m two three", not "m
twenty-three".

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.1 — Reading the mine map"}
1. M has 3 rows and 4 columns, so its size is **3 × 4**. It has 3 × 4 = 12
   entries.
2. $m_{14}$ is in row 1, column 4: **1** gem.
3. $m_{32}$ is in row 3, column 2: **7** gems. $m_{23}$ is in row 2, column 3:
   **0** gems. Swapping the two numbers gives another tile.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.2 — An enemy table"}
An RPG keeps its enemies in a 2 × 3 matrix E. Row 1 is the slime, row 2 the
troll; the columns are HP, damage and speed:
$$E = \begin{bmatrix} 40 & 10 & 4 \\ 60 & 20 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$

1. The damage of the troll is in row 2, column 2: $e_{22} = 20$.
2. $e_{13} = 4$ is the speed of the slime.
3. To add a third enemy, the designer adds a row: E becomes 3 × 3.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing the size as "columns × rows". The size of M is 3 × 4, not 4 × 3. A
spreadsheet makes this mistake easy: the cell C2 is column C, row 2, but the
entry $a_{23}$ is row 2, column 3.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your own level as a matrix"}
On squared paper, draw a small level of 3 rows and 3 tiles. Write a number of
coins in each tile.

1. Write the level as a matrix L. What is its size?
2. Circle $l_{32}$ and $l_{23}$. Are they the same tile?

*Your result:* the matrix L, its size, and the two circled entries.
:::

## 9.2 A position is a small matrix: row and column vectors

The player stands at P = (3, 5). A vector is also a matrix, with only one row
or only one column (@fig-rowcol).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 9.2 — Row vector, column vector and transpose"}
A **row vector** is a matrix with one row (size 1 × n). A **column vector**
is a matrix with one column (size n × 1). The **transpose** $A^T$ of a matrix
A turns its rows into columns: the entry $a_{ij}$ moves to row *j*, column
*i*. A matrix of size m × n has a transpose of size n × m.
:::

![P = (3, 5) as a row vector and as a column vector. The transpose turns one into the other.](images/row-column.png){#fig-rowcol width=94%}

$$\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}^T = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$

Game engines and the textbook of this course write positions and directions
as **column vectors**. From lecture 10 on, a matrix multiplies a column
vector to move a point.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.3 — Three enemies in one matrix"}
Three enemies stand at (2, 1), (5, 3) and (0, 4). The game keeps their
positions as the columns of one 2 × 3 matrix:
$$P = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$$

1. Row 1 holds the x-coordinates, row 2 the y-coordinates.
2. Column 2 is the second enemy: (5, 3).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.4 — The transpose of the enemy table"}
The enemy table E of Example 9.2 is 2 × 3.

1. Its transpose $E^T$ is 3 × 2: the rows (40, 10, 4) and (60, 20, 2) become
   columns.
2. In $E^T$ each row is a stat: row 1 is HP (40, 60), row 2 is damage
   (10, 20), row 3 is speed (4, 2).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that the transpose changes the numbers. It only moves them: the
same 6 numbers, in other places.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Transpose the mine map"}
Write the transpose $M^T$ of the mine map M of section 9.1.

1. What is the size of $M^T$?
2. Which number is in row 3, column 2 of $M^T$? Find it in M too.

*Your result:* $M^T$, its size and the entry you found twice.
:::

## 9.3 Two rounds, one total: adding matrices

A puzzle game shows the points of two players (rows) in three levels
(columns). Round 1 gives one matrix of points, the bonus round another. The
total of each player in each level is the sum of two entries in the same
place (@fig-add).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 9.3 — Matrix addition and subtraction"}
Two matrices of the **same size** are added entry by entry:
$(A + B)_{ij} = a_{ij} + b_{ij}$. Subtraction works the same way:
$(A - B)_{ij} = a_{ij} - b_{ij}$. The result has the same size. Matrices of
different sizes cannot be added.
:::

![Adding two 2 × 3 matrices: every entry with the entry in the same place.](images/matrix-add.png){#fig-add width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.5 — Points after the bonus round"}
$$\begin{bmatrix} 120 & 80 & 50 \\ 90 & 60 & 40 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 30 & 20 & 10 \\ 10 & 40 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 150 & 100 & 60 \\ 100 & 100 & 40 \end{bmatrix}$$

1. Both matrices are 2 × 3, so the sum exists and is 2 × 3.
2. Player 1 in level 2: 80 + 20 = 100.
3. Player 2 in level 3: 40 + 0 = 40.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.6 — Moving three enemies at once"}
The enemies of Example 9.3 each take one step. The steps are the columns of
D:
$$P + D = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$

1. Enemy 1: (2, 1) + (1, 0) = (3, 1). This is vector addition (lecture 3),
   done for all enemies at once.
2. Enemy 3: (0, 4) + (0, −2) = (0, 2).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Adding a 2 × 3 matrix to a 3 × 2 matrix. There is no entry in the same place
for every number, so the sum does not exist. Check the sizes first.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/matrix-lab.html" poster="sims/matrix-lab.png" title="Matrix Lab: add, subtract and multiply by a number" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Add in Matrix Lab"}
Open **Matrix Lab** (above, or scan the QR code).

1. Choose A + B. Tap three entries of the result and write each sum.
2. Choose A − B and tap one entry. Then press "B: 2 × 3" to make B a 3 × 2
   matrix. What does the lab say?

*Your result:* four calculations and one sentence about the sizes.
:::

## 9.4 Hard mode: multiplying a matrix by a number

In hard mode, every enemy of the RPG has 1.5 times its HP, damage and speed.
The designer does not change the table number by number: the game multiplies
the whole matrix by 1.5 (@fig-scale).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 9.4 — A number times a matrix"}
To multiply a matrix A by a number k (a **scalar**), multiply every entry by
k: $(kA)_{ij} = k\,a_{ij}$. The size does not change.
:::

![Hard mode multiplies every entry of the stats matrix by 1.5.](images/matrix-scale.png){#fig-scale width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.7 — The stats in hard mode"}
$$1.5 \begin{bmatrix} 40 & 10 & 4 \\ 60 & 20 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 60 & 15 & 6 \\ 90 & 30 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

1. The troll's HP: 1.5 × 60 = 90.
2. The slime's damage: 1.5 × 10 = 15.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.8 — Negative numbers and subtraction"}
1. A velocity (3, −1) as a column vector, times 2, gives (6, −2): the same
   rule as scaling a vector in lecture 3.
2. Times −1, a matrix gets the opposite signs: −1 × (3, −1) = (−3, 1).
3. So A − B is the same as A + (−1)B.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Multiplying only one row or one column. The number multiplies **every** entry
of the matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · k × A in Matrix Lab"}
In **Matrix Lab**, choose k × A.

1. Set k = 1.5 and tap two entries of the result. Write each product.
2. Set k = −1. What happens to every sign?

*Your result:* two products and one sentence about k = −1.
:::

## 9.5 The matrix that the engine keeps for every object

A game engine keeps, for every object in the scene, one **square** matrix of
size 4 × 4. It is the object's **transformation matrix**: its 16 numbers say
where the object is, how it is turned and how big it is (@fig-trs). You read
it now; lectures 11 to 14 show how it is built.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 9.5 — Square matrix and main diagonal"}
A **square matrix** has as many rows as columns (2 × 2, 3 × 3, 4 × 4). Its
**main diagonal** is the entries $a_{11}, a_{22}, a_{33}, \ldots$ from the
top left to the bottom right.
:::

![The 4 × 4 matrix of a crate. The last column holds its position; the top-left 3 × 3 part holds its turn and size.](images/transform-matrix.png){#fig-trs width=96%}

In the matrix of an object that is not turned and has size 1, the main
diagonal holds 1s, and the last column holds the position (x, y, z) and a 1.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.9 — Where is the crate?"}
$$T = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

1. T is square: 4 × 4. Its main diagonal is 1, 1, 1, 1.
2. The last column is (4, 2, 7, 1). The crate stands at **(4, 2, 7)**.
3. The crate moves 2 units along +x: only $t_{14}$ changes, from 4 to 6.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
Matrix4x4 m = transform.localToWorldMatrix;  // the object's 4 × 4 matrix
Vector4 last = m.GetColumn(3);               // (4, 2, 7, 1)
float x = m[0, 3];                           // row 0, column 3: 4
```
`Matrix4x4` is Unity's 4 × 4 matrix. `GetColumn(3)` gives the last column.
Code counts rows and columns from 0, so `m[0, 3]` is the entry $t_{14}$ of
the maths.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.10 — Code numbers and maths numbers"}
1. `m[1, 3]` is row 1, column 3 in code: row 2, column 4 in maths, so
   $t_{24} = 2$, the y-coordinate.
2. `m[2, 2]` is $t_{33}$, on the main diagonal: 1.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Two objects, two matrices"}
A tree has the matrix with rows (1, 0, 0, 3), (0, 1, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1, 5),
(0, 0, 0, 1). A lamp has rows (1, 0, 0, −2), (0, 1, 0, 4), (0, 0, 1, 5),
(0, 0, 0, 1).

1. Write both matrices and mark their last columns.
2. Where is each object? Which one is higher (larger y)?

*Your result:* the two positions and the higher object.
:::

## Case study: Gem Grid

*Gem Grid* is a made-up mining game. The mine map is the 3 × 4 matrix M of
section 9.1: rows (2, 0, 5, 1), (4, 3, 0, 6) and (1, 7, 2, 0). At night, a
bonus layer N adds gems: rows (1, 1, 0, 0), (0, 2, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 3, 1).
In hard mode every tile has twice the gems: 2M. The player must read the
right tile, add the night layer, and double the map. The Game challenge of
the interactive lesson uses these numbers. In the mini-game below you play
five rounds.

{{< sim file="sims/gem-grid.html" poster="sims/gem-grid.png" title="Gem Grid: read, add and double the mine map" kind="game" height="640" >}}

## Further reading

Dunn and Parberry, *3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development*,
2nd ed., Chapter 4 (Introduction to Matrices): matrix dimensions and
notation, square matrices, the transpose, and row and column vectors.

## Exercises

1. A matrix has 2 rows and 5 columns. What is its size, and how many entries
   does it have?
2. In the mine map M, what is $m_{21}$? What is $m_{12}$?
3. In the enemy table E (rows (40, 10, 4) and (60, 20, 2)), which entry is
   the speed of the troll?
4. Write P = (−2, 6) as a column vector and as a row vector.
5. A matrix is 4 × 2. What is the size of its transpose?
6. Write the transpose of the matrix with rows (1, 2, 3) and (4, 5, 6).
7. Add the matrices with rows (3, 1), (0, 2) and rows (1, 1), (4, −2).
8. Can a 3 × 2 matrix and a 2 × 3 matrix be added? Why?
9. Three coins are at (1, 1), (4, 0) and (2, 5). They all fall by 1 unit.
   Write the position matrix and the step matrix, and add them.
10. Compute 3A for A with rows (2, 0) and (−1, 4).
11. In hard mode the stats are 1.5 E. What is the HP of the slime (40)?
12. Compute A − B for A with rows (5, 2) and B with rows (1, 3).
13. Which of these are square: 2 × 2, 2 × 3, 4 × 4, 1 × 1?
14. An object's matrix has the last column (−3, 1, 8, 1). Where is the
    object?
15. *Gem Grid*: how many gems are in row 1, column 3 of M + N? And of 2M?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. 2 × 5; 10 entries.
2. $m_{21} = 4$; $m_{12} = 0$.
3. $e_{23} = 2$.
4. Column: rows −2 and 6. Row: (−2  6).
5. 2 × 4.
6. Rows (1, 4), (2, 5), (3, 6): a 3 × 2 matrix.
7. Rows (4, 2) and (4, 0).
8. No: the sizes are different.
9. Rows (1, 4, 2) and (1, 0, 5) plus rows (0, 0, 0) and (−1, −1, −1) gives rows (1, 4, 2) and (0, −1, 4).
10. Rows (6, 0) and (−3, 12).
11. 1.5 × 40 = 60.
12. (4, −1).
13. 2 × 2, 4 × 4 and 1 × 1.
14. At (−3, 1, 8).
15. M + N: 5 + 0 = 5. 2M: 2 × 5 = 10.
:::
